Reference data

Source: vignettes/reference-data.Rmd
reference-data.Rmd

Eight of the tests compare a record with reference data from a shipped layer: points (capitals, country and province centroids, biodiversity institutions, artificial hotspots) and polygons (land, urban areas, countries). The ninth, range, needs species range polygons, which the user supplies (Custom reference points and polygons). This article lists where each layer comes from, how the package’s own reference data compare with CoordinateCleaner’s, how much the choice of land scale changes the sea test, and how the reference version is recorded with the flags. Installation is covered in Get started.

The layers 

library(OccurrenceCleaner)

ri <- reference_info()
Layer Source Version / snapshot Retrieved

land_50 Natural Earth 4.1.0 2026-10-09
land_10 Natural Earth 5.1.1 2026-10-09
countries_50 Natural Earth 5.1.1 2026-10-09
urban_50 Natural Earth 4.1.0 2026-10-09

admin0_10 Natural Earth 5.1.1 2026-10-09
admin1_10 Natural Earth 5.1.1 2026-10-09

world_borders thematicmapping.org World Borders Dataset 0.3 (2008-07-30) 2026-10-11
geolocate GEOLocate web service 2026-10-11 2026-10-11
institutions GBIF GRSciColl 2026-10-09 2026-10-09
institutions_wikidata Wikidata 2026-10-10 2026-10-10
institutions_wikipedia Wikipedia, lists of natural history museums 7 page revisions (below) 2026-10-11
institutions_geonames GeoNames 2026-10-10 2026-10-10
institutions_bgci BGCI GardenSearch 2026-10-10 2026-10-10
institutions_index_herbariorum Index Herbariorum (New York Botanical Garden) 2026-10-13 2026-10-13
institutions_gbif_registry GBIF registry, publishing organisations 2026-10-13 2026-10-13
institutions_coordinatecleaner_list CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1 institution list, placed by Wikidata, OpenStreetMap (Nominatim) and GeoNames 3.0.1 2026-10-13
aohi AHOI (Park et al. 2023) 2022-10-10 2026-10-10
habitat IRMNG (Rees 2026) 2026-10-06 2026-10-10

reference_info() lists each source’s version, file name, download URL, SHA-256 checksum and licence.

  • The factbook version is the shortened commit hash of the factbook.json mirror. reference_info() gives the full hash.

  • Wikipedia lists use fixed page revisions: en 1376233148; de 267938927; fr 240149609; nl 69876533; pt 71307420; ar 76691072; eo 9165115.

  • The Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera (IRMNG) is cited as: Rees, T. (compiler) (2026), The Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera, available from irmng.org at VLIZ.

  • The layer name aohi follows CoordinateCleaner’s cc_aohi(). The inventory itself uses the abbreviation AHOI.

The tests use the following layers:

test reference data
capital CIA World Factbook capital coordinates, Natural Earth populated places: admin-0 capitals, alternative capitals and capitals of dependent territories
centroid CIA World Factbook, thematicmapping.org World Borders and GEOLocate country points, Natural Earth admin-0 polygon centroids and label points, admin-1 label points
institution GBIF GRSciColl institutions, Wikidata botanical gardens, natural history museums, zoos, aquaria and herbaria, museums of Wikipedia’s lists of natural history museums, BGCI gardens, Index Herbariorum herbaria and GBIF publishing organisations, with coordinates, and every further institution of CoordinateCleaner’s table placed from Wikidata, OpenStreetMap or GeoNames
gbif_headquarters one fixed point, 12.58 E, 55.67 N
aohi Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (Park et al. 2023), 308 points
sea Natural Earth land at 1:110 million (default), 1:50 million or 1:10 million
urban Natural Earth urban areas 1:50 million
country_mismatch Natural Earth admin-0 countries 1:50 million
sea_nonmarine, land_marine the land of sea, and genus habitats from the Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera

The sections below give the provenance of each layer: its sources, their licences and retrieval dates, and how the points were matched or placed.

Capitals

The capitals are the capital “geographic coordinates” of the CIA World Factbook, the source of CoordinateCleaner’s capitals, read from the same factbook.json mirror: one point per country profile, 232 in all. The Natural Earth admin-0 capitals, alternative capitals and capitals of dependent territories (243) are added with extension TRUE.

Country and province centroids

The country centroids come from the three sources CoordinateCleaner’s table is compiled from, each taken from the source itself:

  • The “Geographic coordinates” of the CIA World Factbook (public domain), read from the factbook.json mirror of the Factbook country profiles on 2026-10-11: 275 points.

  • The label points of the World Borders Dataset 0.3 by Bjorn Sandvik, thematicmapping.org, under CC BY-SA, from the GeoJSON conversion of the dataset at github.com/jeffaudi/world-borders-geojson: 246 points.

  • Every point the GEOLocate georeferencing service (geo-locate.org) returns when a country name is entered as country and locality, queried on 2026-10-11 for each country name of the three tables: 548 points. GEOLocate also returns places that carry a country’s name. One such place, Niger State in Nigeria for “Niger”, lies inside another country more than 100 km from the queried one and is left out.

The Natural Earth admin-0 polygon centroids, computed on the sphere, and label points (516) are added with extension TRUE. The province centroids are the Natural Earth admin-1 label points.

Land, countries and urban areas

The land, country and urban-area polygons are Natural Earth layers at the scales the table above gives. All Natural Earth layers are in the public domain; the Natural Earth terms of use say that “No permission is needed to use Natural Earth.”

Institutions

The institutions come from the bulk export of GBIF’s Global Registry of Scientific Collections (GRSciColl), retrieved on 2026-10-09: 10,002 institutions, of which 6,085 have coordinates. The five of these that the zero test would flag are left out: four are registered within 0.14 degrees of (0, 0), although they are in Portugal, Nigeria, Turkey and Taiwan, and one has a longitude of exactly 0. Kept, they would mark every record at (0, 0) as lying at an institution as well. GRSciColl absorbed the Global Registry of Biodiversity Repositories (GRBio) in 2018 and is synchronised weekly with Index Herbariorum. GBIF publishes the registry through its open API and states no separate licence for it.

The institution table includes locations from Wikidata, Wikipedia, GeoNames and Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI). The source column of reference_points("institution") identifies the source of each point.

Wikidata (CC0, queried 2026-10-10) supplies coordinates for:

  • Botanical gardens, natural history museums, zoos, public aquaria and herbaria, including items in subclasses of these categories.

  • Museums whose main subject or field of work is a natural-history discipline, such as geology, paleontology, zoology or botany.

  • Museums in Wikipedia’s English “List of natural history museums”, which supplies CoordinateCleaner’s Wikipedia entries, and its Arabic, Dutch, Esperanto, French, German and Portuguese counterparts.

The Wikipedia lists contain 2,331 entries (CC BY-SA 4.0, retrieved 2026-10-11). Entries are matched to Wikidata through their linked articles. Entries without an article are matched when a single museum item in the same country has the corresponding name and lies within 25 km of the named town.

After removing duplicate Wikidata items, these sources provide 7,810 points: 3,263 botanical gardens, 1,835 museums, 2,609 zoos and aquaria, and 103 herbaria. None has zero coordinates.

Museums without their own Wikidata coordinates are located using the place named in the Wikipedia entry. This is either the Wikidata location of a linked town or university, checked against the entry’s country, or a GeoNames populated place matching the named town (CC BY 4.0). This adds 700 points, including 385 from the English list. Entries without a town are omitted.

The three GeoNames locations in CoordinateCleaner’s table come from the GeoNames country files (CC BY 4.0).

BGCI’s GardenSearch map, retrieved for all countries on 2026-10-10, lists 3,765 gardens. Of these, 3,653 have coordinates; removing one at zero coordinates leaves 3,652 points. These are used under the BGCI terms.

Two further registries were downloaded in full on 2026-10-13:

  • Index Herbariorum, the New York Botanical Garden’s herbarium registry, provides locations for 4,805 herbaria. The table adds the 1,062 for which GRSciColl lacks coordinates under the same herbarium code.

  • The GBIF registry provides coordinates for 2,468 of its 3,639 publishing organisations. All 2,468 are added.

The remaining institutions with coordinates in CoordinateCleaner’s table are located using their name, city and country. An institution is already represented if an entry matches its name, its full Index Herbariorum name, or an alternative or collection name recorded by GRSciColl.

Each remaining institution is looked up in this order:

  1. Wikidata, using its full name or the part before the first comma.

  2. OpenStreetMap through Nominatim, accepting a result that matches at least half the institution’s name words or lies within 25 km of CoordinateCleaner’s point.

  3. GeoNames, using the city listed by CoordinateCleaner or GRSciColl.

When several candidates are returned, the candidate nearest CoordinateCleaner’s point is selected. Coordinates come from the selected source.

If these searches find no location, the institution is considered represented when an existing point lies within 25 km and matches at least 60% of its name words. Otherwise, it is assigned to the populated place mentioned in its name or, as a last resort, the populated place in its country nearest CoordinateCleaner’s point. These entries have source = "CoordinateCleaner list"; master_source records how they were located.

Genus habitats

The habitat tests sea_nonmarine and land_marine use genus classifications from the Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera (IRMNG), supplied as a Darwin Core archive dated 2026-10-06 under CC BY 4.0. IRMNG records marine, brackish, freshwater and terrestrial flags for each name. Following the rule in reference_habitat(), the package classifies 296,474 genera as nonmarine and 21,891 as exclusively marine, with kingdom used to distinguish names.

The citation is: Rees, T. (compiler) (2026). The Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera. Available from irmng.org at VLIZ.

Artificial hotspots

The Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (AHOI; Park, Xie, Thammavong, Tulaiha and Feng, 2023) identifies coordinates that recur most often in GBIF records and records why they recur. The authors’ Dryad deposit, released under CC0, supplies 308 points with coordinates: 154 for plants, 51 for birds, 51 for insects and 52 for mammals.

CoordinateCleaner’s bundled aohi table contains 309 points. The two datasets share 303 points; differences involve a few bird locations and one plant latitude, recorded as 42.26° N in CoordinateCleaner and 42.20° N in the deposit.

Scripts in the source repository’s data-raw/ directory rebuild the layers from their source datasets.

How the reference data differ from CoordinateCleaner’s

The package’s reference points describe the same places as CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1’s countryref and institutions tables, but they are not the same tables. Counts as of 2026-10-13, the retrieval date of the last two institution registries:

gazetteer CoordinateCleaner OccurrenceCleaner
capitals 225 (one per ISO3 code) 475: 232 Factbook capitals and 243 Natural Earth capitals, alternative capitals and dependent-territory capitals marked as extension
country centroids 660 rows from the CIA World Factbook, thematicmapping.org and GEOLocate 1,585: 1,069 from the same three sources (275 Factbook, 246 World Borders, 548 GEOLocate) and 516 Natural Earth polygon centroids and label points marked as extension
province centroids 4,645 (older Natural Earth admin-1 label points) 4,594 (Natural Earth 5.1.1 admin-1 label points)
institutions 9,773 with coordinates (GRBio, Index Herbariorum, GBIF, BGCI, Wikipedia, GeoNames) 23,895 (6,080 GRSciColl, without the five at zero coordinates, 7,810 Wikidata, 700 Wikipedia, 3,652 BGCI, 3 GeoNames, 1,062 Index Herbariorum, 2,468 GBIF registry, 2,120 for the rest of CoordinateCleaner’s list), of which 16,230 from CoordinateCleaner’s sources

  • Capitals. Of CoordinateCleaner’s 225 capital points, 221 match this package’s Factbook points when rounded to 0.01 degrees. Rounding shifts their positions by up to 523 m. The remaining four reflect Factbook entries that have since changed: Bujumbura to Gitega for Burundi; Buenos Aires from 58°40′ W to 58°22′ W, correcting a location 27 km west of the city; Melekeok to Ngerulmud for Palau; and a 1.8 km coordinate adjustment for Rangoon.

    Natural Earth adds alternative and official capitals, including Cape Town and Bloemfontein alongside Pretoria, Sucre alongside La Paz, Naypyidaw alongside Yangon, and Dodoma alongside Dar es Salaam. Selecting extension = FALSE excludes these additions.

  • Country centroids. Of CoordinateCleaner’s 660 points, 645 match this package’s points exactly. India, Italy and the United Kingdom use World Borders coordinates that changed in version 0.3. GEOLocate no longer returns three points for Macedonia or a point for Guinea located at sea at 10° W, 5° N. The remaining eight points lie between 5 m and 68 km from the nearest point in this package.

    Natural Earth adds polygon centres, which lie a median of 30 km from CoordinateCleaner’s centroids and flag records georeferenced to those centres. Selecting extension = FALSE excludes these additions.

  • Province centroids. CoordinateCleaner uses Natural Earth administrative label points: 4,566 of its 4,645 rows match codes and coordinates in releases 3.3.0, 4.0.0 or 4.1.0. This package uses release 5.1.1. All province points therefore carry extension = FALSE, since they come from the same source.

    Of CoordinateCleaner’s rows, 4,591 match this package’s points exactly. Of the remaining 54, 50 lie more than 10 km from any included point: 15 use coordinates Natural Earth has since changed, and 39 match no tagged release.

  • Institutions. This package represents 9,772 of CoordinateCleaner’s 9,773 institutions, covering every entry with coordinates except one expert group listed in Antarctica. It matches 6,313 by name and another 329 to nearby points with overlapping name words. The remaining 3,130 are located through Wikidata (1,052), OpenStreetMap (646), the town listed by CoordinateCleaner or GRSciColl (684), or a town mentioned in the institution’s name (252). For 496 institutions, searches found no institution location, so the nearest town to CoordinateCleaner’s point is used.

    Coordinates differ because CoordinateCleaner geocoded nearly all its institutions independently. For example, it located 641 of its 712 BGCI gardens from names and addresses; this package uses BGCI’s coordinates. CoordinateCleaner also located 398 Wikipedia museums manually, to 1 km precision.

    Some locations differ substantially. CoordinateCleaner places all Iranian university museums at one point in Isfahan and the Museo Marino of Boca del Río, Veracruz, in Venezuela. Across its institution points, 32% have a point in this package within 100 m, 73% within 1 km and 91% within 5 km.

    Additional Wikidata institutions and museums from Wikipedia’s other language editions carry extension = TRUE. Selecting extension = FALSE restricts the test to CoordinateCleaner’s sources. With CoordinateCleaner installed, its table can also be added at run time (Custom reference points and polygons).

The following example shows how the capital references affect flags for records at alternative or official capitals:

x <- data.frame(city = c("Pretoria", "Cape Town", "La Paz", "Sucre", "Yangon", "Naypyidaw"),
                species = "a",
                decimalLongitude = c(28.19, 18.42, -68.15, -65.26, 96.16, 96.13),
                decimalLatitude = c(-25.75, -33.92, -16.50, -19.04, 16.80, 19.75))
data.frame(city = x$city,
           OccurrenceCleaner = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital,
           CoordinateCleaner = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner")$flag_capital)
#>        city OccurrenceCleaner CoordinateCleaner
#> 1  Pretoria              TRUE              TRUE
#> 2 Cape Town              TRUE             FALSE
#> 3    La Paz              TRUE              TRUE
#> 4     Sucre              TRUE             FALSE
#> 5    Yangon              TRUE              TRUE
#> 6 Naypyidaw              TRUE             FALSE

Cape Town, Sucre and Naypyidaw are flagged only through the Natural Earth extension points; Pretoria, La Paz and Yangon under both. Which list is right depends on what an error looks like: a herbarium sheet in Cape Town georeferenced to the city is as wrong under either reference, and only the extension points catch it.

Extension points

The capital, country centroid and institution tables also contain points from sources CoordinateCleaner does not use, marked extension TRUE:

  • capitals: 243 Natural Earth capitals, alternative capitals and capitals of dependent territories;

  • country centroids: 516 Natural Earth polygon centroids and label points;

  • institutions: 7,665 points, the botanical gardens, natural history museums, zoos, aquaria and herbaria of Wikidata beyond the museums of the English Wikipedia list, and the museums of the Arabic, Dutch, Esperanto, French, German and Portuguese lists.

The tests use them by default. Passing the rows with extension FALSE through gazetteers restricts a test to CoordinateCleaner’s sources; for the capitals above, that leaves Cape Town, Sucre and Naypyidaw unflagged:

g <- reference_points("capital")
data.frame(city = x$city,
           all = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital,
           cc_sources = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital",
                                         gazetteers = list(capital = g[!g$extension, ]))$flag_capital)
#>        city  all cc_sources
#> 1  Pretoria TRUE       TRUE
#> 2 Cape Town TRUE      FALSE
#> 3    La Paz TRUE       TRUE
#> 4     Sucre TRUE      FALSE
#> 5    Yangon TRUE       TRUE
#> 6 Naypyidaw TRUE      FALSE

Land scale and the sea test

The sea test flags records outside the land polygons. It supports Natural Earth land polygons at scales of 1:110 million, 1:50 million and 1:10 million. OccurrenceCleaner defaults to 1:110 million (land_scale = 110). CoordinateCleaner defaults to 1:110 million in cc_sea() and 1:50 million in clean_coordinates(). The 1:10 million layer is downloaded on first use and cached.

The coarse 1:110 million layer smooths the coast and drops small islands; the 1:50 million layer follows the coast more closely. A grid of points over Denmark and the western Baltic shows where the two disagree:

g <- expand.grid(decimalLongitude = seq(7.5, 15.5, by = 0.05),
                 decimalLatitude = seq(54, 58, by = 0.05))
g$species <- "a"
s110 <- flag_occurrences(g, tests = "sea")$flag_sea
s50 <- flag_occurrences(g, tests = "sea", land_scale = 50)$flag_sea
g$verdict <- ifelse(s110 & s50, "sea at both", ifelse(!s110 & !s50, "land at both",
                    ifelse(s110, "sea at 1:110 million only", "sea at 1:50 million only")))
table(g$verdict)
#> 
#>              land at both sea at 1:110 million only  sea at 1:50 million only 
#>                      5765                       519                       783 
#>               sea at both 
#>                      5974
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(g, aes(decimalLongitude, decimalLatitude, fill = verdict)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`land at both` = "#C8B88A", `sea at both` = "#A9C7E0",
                               `sea at 1:110 million only` = "#C0392B", `sea at 1:50 million only` = "#2C3E50")) +
  coord_quickmap(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "longitude", y = "latitude", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical") +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA))

On this grid the two scales disagree for 10 % of the points, all of them along the coast. At 1:110 million Funen, Lolland, Falster, Rügen and Bornholm are missing, so records on them are flagged as at sea (red); the coarse 1:110 million coastline also reaches out into the water, so records in a strip of coastal water count as on land there and are flagged only at 1:50 million (dark). For coastal and island taxa the scale therefore changes a share of the sea flags large enough to see in a tally. The 1:10 million layer is the most detailed of the three:

download_reference("land_10")
f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "sea", land_scale = 10)

The download is checked against the SHA-256 in reference_info() and refused if Natural Earth has published a different file under the same name. The converted layer is stored in tools::R_user_dir("OccurrenceCleaner", "cache"), so it is downloaded once per machine.

Buffers

The buffers are the other half of every proximity test. They default to CoordinateCleaner’s (10 km for capitals, 1 km for centroids and the GBIF headquarters, 100 m for institutions, 0.5 degrees around (0, 0)) and are changed per test:

x <- data.frame(species = "a", decimalLongitude = c(16.37, 16.45), decimalLatitude = c(48.21, 48.21))
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital
#> [1] TRUE TRUE
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital", buffers = list(capital = 2000))$flag_capital
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE

A buffer of 2 km for capitals keeps records from the outer districts of a capital while still removing those placed at the city’s coordinates. The 0.5-degree zero buffer is in degrees, the others in metres.

Recording the reference

Every flagged data frame carries the reference that produced it, with the version of each layer. The printed object shows the short form; flag_reference() returns the full label, which names every layer with its version, snapshot date or page revision:

f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("capital", "sea"), land_scale = 50)
f
#> <occ_flags> 2 records, 2 tests, reference OccurrenceCleaner 0.2.0, land 50
#>   species decimalLongitude decimalLatitude flags flagged_by
#> 1       a            16.37           48.21     8    capital
#> 2       a            16.45           48.21     8    capital
attr(f, "occ_layout_version")
#> [1] 4
The full reference label 
flag_reference(f)
#> [1] "OccurrenceCleaner 0.2.0 (land 50; land_110 4.1.0, land_50 4.1.0, land_10 5.1.1, countries_50 5.1.1, urban_50 4.1.0, places_10 5.1.2, admin0_10 5.1.1, admin1_10 5.1.1, factbook factbook.json 144d6977b2b01ac1cbd220de754c0a005616760b, world_borders 0.3 (2008-07-30), geolocate 2026-10-11, institutions 2026-10-09, institutions_wikidata 2026-10-10, institutions_wikipedia en revision 1376233148; de revision 267938927; fr revision 240149609; nl revision 69876533; pt revision 71307420; ar revision 76691072; eo revision 9165115, institutions_geonames 2026-10-10, institutions_bgci 2026-10-10, institutions_index_herbariorum 2026-10-13, institutions_gbif_registry 2026-10-13, institutions_coordinatecleaner_list 3.0.1, aohi 2022-10-10, habitat 2026-10-06)"

reference = "CoordinateCleaner" stamps the installed CoordinateCleaner version instead. For streamed input the same label is written to the output directory, and a rerun into that directory with a different reference, land scale, set of tests or layout stops with an error, so one output directory never mixes flags from two references.

Choosing a reference

  • reference = "OccurrenceCleaner" (the default) needs no other package, has a version and checksum for every layer, and uses current Natural Earth, GRSciColl, Wikidata, Wikipedia, GeoNames, BGCI, Index Herbariorum, GBIF registry and OpenStreetMap data.

  • Set reference = "CoordinateCleaner" to use CoordinateCleaner’s own reference tables, for example to compare with a published analysis that used it. This requires CoordinateCleaner to be installed and reproduces its flags subject to the differences documented in Compatibility with CoordinateCleaner. The polygon tests also need rnaturalearth, which downloads the Natural Earth layers at run time as CoordinateCleaner does.

Both references use the same buffers and the same geodesic distance, so the difference between them is in the points and polygons only.
